🔔 Can DATA Network bring lasting activity to Sui? 

📣 DATA Network plans to retire its independent chain and run its AI training data registry on Sui, with Walrus handling files. Sui Foundation is investing $30 million in the network. A registry that its backers say already records millions of receipts daily could bring activity to Sui; how much of that translates into recurring SUI demand remains an open question.

⭐️ Sui Foundation’s October 12 announcement  says Trace, a rights registry for AI training data, is joining its stack. Walrus will store encrypted original files and Sui will record programmable rights and settlements. DATA Network’s own chain will eventually close. The foundation says its $30 million commitment makes it the largest institutional holder of the DATA Network, alongside PIP Labs and the DATA Foundation. The statement does not publish a completed migration date or a dollar amount of fees the business expects to pay on Sui. 

⚠️ Trace registers a data contribution, its origin and the rights attached to it. The foundation says the system has processed more than 250 million contributions since a June launch and averages over 3 million receipts a day. Applications named in the announcement include Kled, Numo and Oto. Kled is described as an opt in human data marketplace with more than 1.5 billion records being onboarded. Those are participant supplied operational claims; the release does not contain an independently audited breakdown by customer, chain, fee or paying AI lab. 

🔖 DATA Foundation says Trace settles payments to contributors when their data is licensed. A nurse’s consented account, a dashcam clip or a factory worker’s demonstration might be recorded as training material with use rights. The registry entry is not necessarily the complete source file. Its design separates a claim about who supplied data and who may use it from storage of the bytes. Sui and Walrus are meant to handle those parts after migration.

⚡️ Iran and Iraq aim to increase tourist exchanges to 10 million, minister says

📌 Ahvaz, IRNA – Iran and Iraq have the potential to increase annual tourist exchanges to 10 million people, Tourism Minister Reza Salehi-Amiri said on Wednesday, stressing the need for new planning and stronger cross-border infrastructure to achieve the target.

Speaking upon arrival in southwestern province of Khuzestan, Salehi Amiri identified Khuzestan as a key focus of efforts to expand tourism ties between the neighboring countries, highlighting the province’s potential for land travel, medical tourism and improved border infrastructure.
​
Given existing limitations in air transport, Iran is prioritizing the development of land crossings and road travel through four border provinces – Khuzestan, Ilam, Kermanshah and West Azarbaijan – the minister said.
​
Salehi-Amiri said around 3.6 million Iraqi tourists visit Iran annually, while approximately 3.6 million Iranians travel to Iraq over the same period. These figures do not include the large number of people who travel to Iraq for the annual Arbaeen pilgrimage, he added.
​
The minister described strengthening land-based tourism as a major focus of his visit to Khuzestan, saying officials would examine the province’s capabilities to facilitate greater movement between the two countries.
​
He also stressed the importance of improving border facilities and organizing medical tourism services in the province as part of broader efforts to expand bilateral tourism.
​
Achieving the proposed target of 10 million tourist exchanges will require new planning and the development of fresh prospects for tourism cooperation, Salehi-Amiri said.

HeartWise

I want to live my life. Ideally, all the possible versions of it.

Sometimes the chance to leave feels better than leaving itself. Until you make a decision, another life remains somewhere within reach: in it, you’re braver, more interesting, doing work that suits you—and probably sleeping better. That life has no utility bills or miserable Tuesdays yet. It’s hard for the life you’re actually living to compete.

In *The Sickness Unto Death*, Kierkegaard wrote about the despair of losing yourself in possibility. The imagination keeps offering new paths, while the task of becoming someone in particular gets put off. The options multiply, but none of them lead to action. Yet Kierkegaard saw the opposite extreme as painful too: believing that nothing else is possible. We have to hold on to both an open future and the limits of our own lives.

Maybe this is what makes choosing so frightening: we have to give up several appealing versions of ourselves, with no guarantee that the one we keep will be the best. You can love your work and still grieve the career you never pursued. You can be happy with someone and know that other encounters might have changed your life, too. Unlived possibilities are hard to let go of. They have one enormous advantage over the life you’re living: they never had to become real.
